what_it_does: Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) is a set of standards that lets Ethernet — the technology behind most wired networks — deliver data with guaranteed, predictable timing, which is critical in factory automation, cars, and other cyber-physical systems where a late packet can mean a physical failure. One key TSN mechanism is the Time-Aware Shaper (TAS), which opens and closes gates in front of each network queue on a precise schedule so that high-priority frames always get through on time. The problem is that traditional TAS hardware stores a separate rule for every individual frame that will ever pass through, which can require tens of megabits (millions of bits) of on-chip memory — more than most network switches have available. METAS (Memory-Efficient TAS) flips the approach: instead of pre-storing per-frame rules, it stores just one persistent rule per data flow (a stream of related frames) and generates the frame-level timing rules on the fly as each frame arrives. On a prototype built in an FPGA (a reprogrammable chip), this cuts memory from about 14 megabits down to roughly 288 kilobits for 1,024 simultaneous flows — a roughly 50x reduction — while still meeting microsecond timing deadlines.
